strengths: The paper addresses an important practical question: whether architectural support for arbitrary resolutions translates into accurate resolution transfer. Separating sampling-rate changes from changes in frequency content provides a useful experimental framework.

The evaluation covers three PDE datasets, multiple training and testing resolutions, spectral diagnostics, rollout artifacts, and several corrective approaches. The results document substantial failures in some FNO configurations.
The multi-resolution sampling experiments provide useful practical evidence that mixing predominantly coarse data with some finer data can improve performance across the tested resolutions.
weaknesses: The conclusions substantially exceed the evidence. Failure to recover previously unseen high-frequency content is distinct from failure to approximate a continuous operator accurately across discretizations. Band-limited methods can achieve useful resolution transfer without reconstructing every frequency. Indeed, Figure 26 reports nearly resolution-independent Navier–Stokes errors for CNO/CROP and explicitly states that they outperform both FNO and multi-resolution training, which undermines the broad dismissal of these approaches.

The spectral diagnostics do not establish aliasing as the cause of the observed errors. Excess high-frequency energy can also reflect approximation error, boundary treatment, or unstable rollouts. Normalization by small ground-truth spectral energies can magnify weak spectral tails. The paper needs absolute residual spectra, clearly defined normalization, and controlled tests distinguishing aliasing from other errors; matching average energy spectra alone also does not establish accurate predictions.

The physics-informed comparison is insufficient to support the negative conclusion about PINO-style methods. The manuscript does not specify residual discretization, derivative computation, boundary enforcement, loss normalization, or whether physics constraints are evaluated on finer grids than the supervised data. Testing weights of 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 without these details does not establish an adequate comparison, especially when the physics-informed models already underperform on their training resolution.

Baseline reliability remains unresolved. Figure 25 includes a CNO configuration that fails to converge and other configurations with very large errors. Hyperparameters are selected at one resolution and transferred to the others. Appendix I includes a useful mode-count ablation, but does not clearly explain how spectral weights unavailable during coarse-grid training are handled at finer resolutions. These issues require validation before failures can be attributed broadly to the model families.

The filtered-data experiments require a more careful interpretation. Filtering inputs and outputs independently generally changes the effective mapping for nonlinear PDEs; filtering need not commute with the solution operator. Consequently, the frequency-extrapolation experiments can conflate discretization transfer with changes in the learning problem. A controlled operator with known spectral behavior would strengthen the causal argument.

Multi-resolution training has limited methodological novelty relative to the cited multi-resolution and multi-fidelity work. Its strongest results concern resolutions represented during training, while the paper itself reports inconsistent improvements at omitted resolutions. The efficiency evidence includes epoch timings, but does not establish end-to-end savings at matched accuracy and training budgets or measure data-generation costs. For Navier–Stokes, changing batch size and learning rate between single- and multi-resolution training further confounds the comparison.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting are inadequate for a study making broad negative claims. Dataset sizes and splits, architecture configurations, preprocessing and resampling details, rollout protocols, and repeated-run uncertainty are not sufficiently specified. The provided manuscript has no usable code link. Reporting inconsistencies also need correction: the mixture (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2) is not a valid proportion vector, and the loss-change factors stated in Section 3.2 do not agree with Figure 16.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical question: whether neural operators remain accurate when inference resolution differs from training resolution. Distinguishing sampling-rate changes from changes in frequency content provides a useful experimental framework.

Experiments cover three standard PDE datasets, multiple training and testing resolutions, spectral diagnostics, physics-informed objectives, and band-limited baselines. The results document meaningful failure cases, including severe instability under some resolution changes.

The multi-resolution training experiments provide useful practical evidence that mixing predominantly coarse samples with some finer samples can improve performance across the represented resolutions.
weaknesses: The central conclusions exceed the evidence. Accurate evaluation on a finer grid does not necessarily require recovering previously unseen high-frequency content; these are distinct objectives with different assumptions. Although Section 3 initially separates them, the paper subsequently treats failure to recover the full spectrum as invalidating multi-resolution inference generally. The experiments establish brittleness in particular configurations, rather than a general inability of machine-learned operators to generalize across resolutions.

The paper's own results substantially qualify its negative claims. Figure 26 shows nearly resolution-independent Navier–Stokes errors for CNO and CROP, and its caption explicitly states that these methods outperform multi-resolution training on average. Figure 16 also shows approximately unchanged Burgers errors across several unseen resolutions. These successes require explicit reconciliation with the claim that neither band-limited learning nor existing operators enable accurate multi-resolution inference, including a clearly defined accuracy criterion.

Spectral discrepancies alone do not identify aliasing. Excess high-frequency energy can also reflect approximation error, boundary treatment, optimization instability, or how Fourier modes are handled across resolutions. Section 3.1 additionally describes prediction spectra while the figures report residual spectra, and normalization by the unfiltered target spectrum can magnify errors where target energy is small. Absolute spectral errors, integrated error measures for the controlled experiments, and direct aliasing controls are needed to establish the proposed mechanism.

The negative baseline evidence is insufficiently controlled. Hyperparameters are selected at one resolution and transferred to others; the CNO Burgers baseline even fails to converge at one training resolution. The physics-informed comparison tests only three nonzero loss weights, without adequately specifying residual discretization, relative loss scales, or higher-resolution physics supervision. These results do not convincingly distinguish limitations of the approaches from unsuccessful implementations or optimization settings.

The proposed remedy has limited methodological novelty, and its evaluation does not establish broad resolution generalization. The paper acknowledges prior dual-resolution training, while its strongest results include every evaluated resolution in training; pairwise training does not consistently improve unseen resolutions. Comparisons also give the proposed method additional resolution-specific supervision, and Navier–Stokes training changes both batch size and learning rate. Matched-supervision and matched-compute controls are needed to isolate the benefit.

Reproducibility and efficiency claims remain under-supported. The manuscript omits important dataset split sizes, architecture settings, random-seed variability, and detailed physics-loss implementations. Average pixel count and epoch timing do not establish end-to-end data-generation savings, particularly without testing independently generated coarse simulations. The reported resolution mixture (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2) also does not sum to one. These gaps matter for a paper whose contribution rests primarily on empirical reassessment.

strengths: Addresses an important practical question: accepting inputs at arbitrary resolutions does not guarantee accurate resolution transfer.
Separating changes in sampling resolution from changes in frequency content provides a useful experimental framework.
Experiments cover three standard PDE datasets, multiple training and testing resolutions, spectral diagnostics, rollout artifacts, and a Fourier-mode ablation.
Multi-resolution training offers a simple practical mitigation, with encouraging accuracy and training-cost tradeoffs, particularly for Darcy flow.
weaknesses: The central conclusions exceed the evidence. Failure to recover frequencies absent from training is distinct from failure to approximate the same band-limited operator on a finer grid. The manuscript recognizes this distinction experimentally but repeatedly conflates the two when declaring band-limited methods ineffective and generalizing its findings to machine-learned operators broadly.

The paper's own results qualify its negative conclusions. Figure 26 shows nearly resolution-independent Navier–Stokes errors for CNO and CROP, and its caption explicitly reports lower losses than multi-resolution training. Figure 16 also contains successful FNO transfers. These results support conditional failure modes, rather than a general rejection of zero-shot resolution transfer.

Spectral evidence needs stronger interpretation and controls. Normalizing residual energy by small high-frequency ground-truth energy can magnify discrepancies without establishing their practical significance. Spectral mismatch alone does not identify aliasing, and matching energy spectra does not establish accurate spatial predictions. Absolute spectral errors, relative solution errors, and controlled anti-aliasing experiments would strengthen the claims.

The physics-informed comparison does not establish a faithful test of the cited super-resolution mechanism. The manuscript does not specify higher-resolution residual evaluation, derivative discretization, boundary treatment, or loss normalization. Testing only three nonzero loss weights, with models sometimes failing even at their training resolution, cannot distinguish optimization or implementation problems from a limitation of physics-informed operator learning.

Baseline quality and comparison controls are insufficient. CNO diverges on the lowest-resolution Burgers setting and performs poorly elsewhere. Hyperparameters are selected at one resolution and reused across resolutions. Navier–Stokes multi-resolution training also changes batch size and reduces the learning rate from 1e-2 to 1e-5, confounding attribution without matched controls.

The proposed remedy has limited demonstrated novelty beyond the cited multi-resolution active-learning work. Comparisons against that approach, compute-matched training strategies, and multi-resolution CNO/CROP are missing. Training on every evaluated resolution demonstrates coverage of those resolutions, but does not establish generalization to unseen ones.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete: dataset counts and splits, detailed architecture configurations, temporal prediction protocols, resampling procedures, and repeated-seed variability are not adequately specified. The stated mixture (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2) is not a valid proportion vector. Data-generation savings are inferred from pixel counts rather than measured using independently generated coarse simulations.

strengths: Addresses an important practical question: whether resolution-independent architectures deliver accurate predictions when deployed beyond their training resolution.
The separation of sampling-rate changes from frequency-content changes is useful, and spectral diagnostics reveal errors that aggregate spatial losses can obscure.

The experimental study is extensive, covering three PDE datasets, several operator approaches, mode-count and anti-aliasing ablations, alternative downsampling methods, and three-seed Darcy experiments.
Multi-resolution training provides a practical mitigation, with measured training-time reductions relative to training exclusively at the highest resolution.
weaknesses: The central conclusions exceed the evidence. Discretization consistency, accurate inference within a resolved bandwidth, and recovery of previously unresolved frequencies are different requirements. Failure at the third does not invalidate the first two. The paper acknowledges that CNO accurately preserves its supported bandwidth, yet characterizes band-limited approaches as ineffective for multi-resolution inference.

The reported results do not uniformly support failure of zero-shot inference. In Figure 16, the Burgers model trained at resolution 128 has approximately the same MSE at resolutions 128, 256, and 512. The paper needs explicit accuracy criteria and comparisons against interpolated coarse predictions and resolution-matched models, rather than interpreting any spectral discrepancy as failure.

Spectral mismatch is not sufficient evidence of aliasing. Approximation error, spectral truncation, and optimization failure can also produce mismatched spectra. The normalized residual metric lacks a precise mathematical definition and stabilization details; division by small high-frequency target energies can exaggerate errors. Absolute spectral errors and controlled demonstrations of frequency folding are needed to substantiate the proposed mechanism.

The physics-informed comparison does not adequately test the cited corrective approach. It studies a weighted PDE penalty but does not establish that residuals are enforced at finer resolutions, a central mechanism of physics-informed super-resolution. Appendix E also omits residual discretization and boundary-treatment details. Failure with three nonzero loss weights, including poor fitting at the training resolution, cannot establish that physics constraints do not enable resolution transfer.

The proposed remedy has limited novelty relative to the substantial multi-resolution training literature already cited. Its evaluation primarily demonstrates performance at resolutions included during training. Moreover, the FNO mode budget depends on maximum training resolution, and Navier–Stokes training changes batch size and learning rate, complicating attribution of improvements to the data mixture alone.

Reproducibility and efficiency claims need stronger support. Dataset counts, train/validation/test splits, and temporal prediction protocols are insufficiently specified. The repeatedly reported mixture (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2) does not sum to one. Data-generation savings are inferred from downsampled data rather than demonstrated with independently generated coarse simulations, and uncertainty estimates are largely restricted to Darcy.

strengths: Addresses an important practical question: whether resolution-independent architectures actually deliver accurate predictions when inference resolution changes. Separating sampling-rate changes from frequency-content changes provides a useful experimental framework.

The empirical investigation is extensive, covering three PDE datasets, FNO, CNO, CROP, and supplementary DeepONet experiments. Additional studies examine Fourier modes, anti-aliasing nonlinearities, downsampling methods, multiple Darcy seeds, and hardware platforms.

Provides concrete evidence of resolution-transfer degradation in the tested configurations. Multi-resolution training offers practical improvements, and Appendix G reports actual training-time and storage savings rather than relying exclusively on theoretical cost arguments.
weaknesses: The central conclusions exceed the evidence. Resolution-independent evaluation, accurate approximation within a resolved frequency band, and recovery of previously unseen frequencies are different capabilities. Failure to recover frequencies outside a prescribed band does not establish failure of resolution transfer within that band. Section 4.2 acknowledges that CNO accurately preserves the learned band without aliasing, yet treats its missing higher frequencies as evidence against multi-resolution inference generally.

The causal attribution to aliasing is insufficiently established. Spectral disagreement and excess high-frequency energy can reflect approximation error, boundary effects, or optimization failure; they do not by themselves demonstrate frequency folding. Normalizing residual spectra by weak high-frequency ground-truth energy can also magnify small absolute errors. The paper needs precise metric definitions, absolute spectral errors, and controlled diagnostics separating aliasing from other errors. Figure 3's caption describes residual spectra, whereas the accompanying text describes normalized prediction spectra.

The physics-informed comparison does not justify dismissing the broader approach. Appendix E largely refers to prior losses without specifying their discretization, normalization, boundary treatment, or residual evaluation resolution. Testing weights of 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 does not adequately explore potentially different loss scales. Crucially, the paper does not establish that it reproduces the higher-resolution physics supervision relevant to PINO's super-resolution claims.

The multi-resolution comparisons contain material confounds. Appendix H sets Fourier-mode capacity according to the maximum training resolution, so changing the resolution mixture can also change model capacity. Table 1 additionally changes Navier–Stokes batch size and learning rate between training regimes. Matched-capacity and matched-optimization comparisons are needed to isolate the benefits of the data mixture.

The proposed remedy has limited novelty relative to the multi-resolution training and active-learning literature that the paper itself cites. Its strongest results concern resolutions explicitly included in training; dual-resolution experiments show inconsistent benefits at omitted resolutions. This supports a useful training heuristic but falls short of establishing a broadly generalizing solution.

Important reproducibility details remain unclear despite the extensive appendices: dataset counts and splits, precise spectral normalization, and the complete physics-loss implementation are not adequately specified. The reported mixture (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2) does not sum to one and appears repeatedly, including in efficiency tables. Uncertainty estimates are largely restricted to Darcy baseline experiments. These issues, together with the conceptual and comparison problems above, leave the contribution below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important practical question: whether resolution-flexible neural operator architectures actually deliver accurate predictions beyond their training resolution.
Separating changes in sampling resolution from changes in frequency content provides a useful experimental framework. Spectral diagnostics expose artifacts that aggregate spatial errors can obscure.

The empirical investigation is substantial: three PDE datasets, several operator approaches, and appendices examining mode counts, anti-aliasing nonlinearities, downsampling methods, DeepONet, and hardware variation. Three-seed Darcy results support the reproducibility of some observed failures.

Multi-resolution training offers a practical mitigation. The paper reports accuracy improvements alongside measured training-time savings, rather than relying exclusively on theoretical cost arguments.
weaknesses: The central conclusions exceed the evidence. Failure to recover frequencies absent from training is distinct from failure of discretization consistency within a resolved frequency band. CNO's expected band limitation does not invalidate its representation-equivalence properties. The experiments establish failure cases for particular configurations, but do not justify categorical statements that machine-learned operators cannot perform accurate zero-shot resolution transfer.

The spectral analysis does not adequately establish the claimed mechanism. Spectral disagreement alone does not identify aliasing; approximation error, optimization failure, and boundary effects can also produce disagreement. Figure 3 shows substantial high-frequency residuals even at the training resolution, weakening their interpretation as evidence of resolution-transfer failure. Precise metric definitions, absolute spectral errors, and errors restricted to the retained frequency band are needed.

The physics-informed comparison is insufficient to support its broad negative conclusion. Appendix E does not specify residual discretization, boundary and initial-condition enforcement, loss normalization, or whether physics residuals are evaluated above the supervised training resolution—a key capability of PINO-style training. Testing weights of 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 without establishing comparable loss scales may primarily demonstrate unsuccessful optimization.

The proposed remedy has limited novelty: multi-resolution training and closely related approaches are already acknowledged in Section 5. The paper does not compare its allocation strategy against these methods under matched data-generation or training budgets. Moreover, evaluating primarily at resolutions included in the mixed training set establishes performance across seen resolutions, rather than generalization to unseen resolutions.

Important experimental controls remain unresolved. Hyperparameters are selected at one resolution and reused elsewhere; the Navier–Stokes multi-resolution experiments also change batch size and learning rate. Figure 16 contains catastrophic errors reaching 2e11, while Appendix N reports large hardware-dependent variation. These observations warrant implementation and optimization checks before attributing the failures principally to distribution shift.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Dataset sample counts, train/validation/test splits, and model-selection procedures are not clearly specified, and code is deferred until acceptance. The repeatedly reported mixture (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2) is inconsistent with its definition as proportions. Uncertainty estimates cover only a subset of Darcy experiments, leaving the main multi-resolution improvements and larger-dataset findings without comparable statistical support.
